title: Serving tuned models and managing costs

opening.headline: Tuning models have different invocation costs and operational burden. Learn how to compare total costs by dividing training, serving, calling, and maintenance costs.
body: The basic model can be called up immediately at a fixed unit price. Tuned models incur training costs first, the unit call price may be different from the base model, and even after training is completed, operational tasks such as evaluation, retraining, and data management are required. “Tuning makes it cheaper” and “Tuning makes it more expensive” are both conditional claims.

In this class, we will divide costs into four categories: learning, serving, call cost, and maintenance. Then, the monthly cost of the basic model and the tuning model are compared using the equation, and the break-even case where the ranking changes depending on the call volume is confirmed through the instructor's commentary.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the serving method and cost structure of the tuning model
Distinguish between learning, serving, and maintenance costs

screens.title: Tuning models have different invocation costs and operational burden.
screens.lead: Read our discussion of costs for teams looking to adopt tuning. It is good to read while thinking about which side of the argument is correct.

paragraphs: During a team meeting, two captains clashed. One side says that tuning reduces the call cost by shortening the prompt, while the other side says that tuning models become more expensive because the learning cost and unit price vary.

Both claims only tell part of the story. The base model can be called immediately at a fixed price, but the tuning model requires learning costs first and the call price may be different from the base model. Additionally, even after learning is complete, there are operational tasks such as evaluation, retraining, and data archiving.
To compare, you need to break down the costs into categories and calculate the total cost for the same period. This class establishes the framework for that calculation.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Tuning costs don't end with learning. You need to distinguish between which costs are one-time costs and which are ongoing costs.

screens.outro: First, let's think about the comparative data we have now.

screens.title: Recall: unit cost comparison between tuned and basic models
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think for yourself first and then click.

items.prompt: Have you compared the unit price of the tuned model and the unit price of the basic model?
items.answer: The unit price of the call can be read from the provider's price list, and the unit price of the tuned model may be different from the basic model. Comparing only the unit price is only half the picture. The number of tokens per call must also be considered.

items.prompt: Have you included learning costs in your comparison?
items.answer: If you subtract the learning cost and compare only the call price, an illusion will appear that tuning has the advantage. Learning costs are a one-time fixed cost and are reflected over the period of use.

items.prompt: If call volume were ten times what it is now, would the cost rankings be the same?
items.answer: If the proportion of fixed costs and variable costs is different, the ranking changes depending on the call volume. When the call volume is low, the fixed cost is burdensome, and when the call volume is high, the difference in cost per call increases. This is the core of this class.

screens.outro: Let’s break the costs down into four categories.

screens.title: Four branches of cost: learning, serving, call cost, and maintenance.
screens.lead: When you hover over or select an underlined term in the text, an explanation appears. Check the four branches one by one.

visual.alt: This figure shows the total cost of the tuning model divided into four parts: learning, serving, invocation, and maintenance, and grouped into fixed and variable costs.

Number of dataset tokens x number of epochs

data.text: The total cost of a tuning model can be divided into four components. First, learning cost: the number of tokens used during training is calculated by multiplying the dataset token count by the number of epochs. Second, the serving method: Gemini's reinforcement learning tuning uses adapter to reuse the existing serving infrastructure unchanged. Third, call unit price: even after tuning is complete, inference requests continue to incur costs. Fourth, maintenance cost: automatic evaluation triggers batch prediction fees, and costs are also incurred for retraining and data management. Among these, training incurs a one-time cost of fixed cost, while invocation costs scale with the number of requests, amounting to variable cost. The actual cost is read from the provider's pricing table and plugged into the formula.

terms.tip: The token used for learning is the number of dataset tokens multiplied by the number of epochs. The larger the data or more epochs, the higher the cost.
This method adjusts only some weights rather than the entire model. It allows you to reuse existing serving infrastructure while fitting it efficiently.
This is the fee attached to the input and output tokens for each request. The unit price of the tuned model may differ from the base model, so check the price list.
This is an ongoing cost after learning is completed. These include running assessments, retraining, and storing and updating training data and assessment sets.
This is a one-time cost regardless of call volume. You can change it to cost per call by dividing it by the period of use or number of calls.
This cost increases in proportion to the call volume. It is calculated as the product of the number of tokens per call and the unit price.

screens.outro: Let’s compare the monthly costs by putting the four parts into an equation.

screens.title: Monthly cost comparison between base and tuned models
screens.lead: Move the slider to check the comparison expressions one by one. The final value organizes judgments based on scale.

stops.body: The basic model's monthly cost is the call volume multiplied by the cost per call. Cost per call is the sum of the input cost multiplied by the number of input tokens and the output cost multiplied by the number of output tokens. If you fill your prompt with long instructions and examples to get the desired behavior, you'll have a lot of input tokens, which increases the cost per call.

The monthly cost of a tuning model is the training cost divided by the number of months, plus the product of the call volume and the tuning model's cost per call, plus the maintenance cost. Learning costs are reflected by dividing them by the period of time they will be used. To make a fair comparison, the two expressions must have the same period and same call volume.

Tuning allows you to train your model to behave, thereby reducing prompts and examples. The cost per call decreases with fewer input tokens, and the benefit accrues as the call volume increases. Short prompts also help reduce latency.

Another advantage of tuning is that you can tune smaller, cheaper, and faster models to take over certain tasks that the larger model needed to do. In this case, the call price itself is lowered. This benefit is also reflected and compared against the cost per call in Eq.

The unit price and number of tokens in the equation are read from the provider price list and actual log. If you enter a number as an estimate, record the result as an estimate as well. Cost calculations are not done once, but are done again whenever the call volume or unit price changes.

screens.outro: Let’s use the equation to explain the change in ranking according to call volume as an example.

screens.title: Case explanation: Total cost ranking changes depending on call volume
screens.lead: The instructor explains the cost comparison using assumed numbers. Click the Next button to follow the ranking as it changes depending on the call volume.

visual.alt: A graph where the total cost lines of the basic model and tuned model according to call volume intersect at the break-even call volume.

steps.title: When call volume is low
steps.body: View a section of a hypothetical service with low call volume. Tuning models have a fixed cost that divides the learning cost by month, so when there are few calls, this fixed cost dominates the entire system. The basic model is cheap in this segment.

steps.title: When call volume increases
steps.body: As call volume increases, the per-call cost difference accumulates. If you shorten the prompt by tuning, the per-call cost of the tuning model is low, so as more calls are made, the gap between the two total costs decreases and at some point reverses.

steps.title: break even
steps.body: The call volume where the two total cost lines meet breaks even. Above the junction, the tuned model has a lower total cost, and below the junction, the base model has a lower total cost. The breaking point depends on unit cost, prompt length, and learning cost.

steps.title: judgment
steps.body: The decision depends on whether the expected call volume for our service is above or below the threshold. If it is far from the junction, it is easy to judge, and if it is near the junction, the value of quality improvement is also added to the judgment. If you expect the call volume to increase, calculate the distance to the junction in advance.

screens.outro: We will also confirm through examples that learning is not the end of cost structure.

screens.title: Case Commentary: Maintenance costs after learning
screens.lead: The instructor explains and explains examples of missing budgets. Click the Next button to see what's missing.

steps.title: Budget Assumptions
steps.body: One team set a budget based on the belief that learning would be completed once. We only factor in learning costs and call costs, not counting the operational work that follows.

steps.title: Change in input distribution
steps.body: As we operated, the distribution of user input changed. The tuning model's performance may then differ from the initial evaluation results, requiring it to be re-evaluated and retrained if necessary.

steps.title: Cost of evaluation
steps.body: If you configure assessments to run automatically, a batch prediction fee is charged for running the assessment service. The evaluation is not just one time, it is repeated with each change and re-learning, so it should be reflected in the monthly cost.

steps.title: data management
steps.body: Storing and updating training data and evaluation sets is also a cost. If you lose data, you cannot retrain. There is also the cost of administrative staff time.

steps.title: lesson
steps.body: Tuning costs don't end with learning. By building maintenance items for evaluation, retraining, and data management into your budget from the beginning, you can avoid running out of money later.

screens.outro: Lastly, let me summarize the main points.

screens.title: Key theorems and connections
screens.lead: Organize the serving and cost of tuning models. As you read, think about the call volume of our service.

paragraphs: The total cost is calculated by dividing it into four parts: learning, serving, calling, and maintaining. Training is a one-time fixed cost, and learning tokens are the number of data tokens multiplied by the number of epochs. Calls are a variable cost proportional to call volume.

Tuning can lower the cost per call by reducing the prompts or replacing them with a smaller model. On the other hand, if call volume is low, fixed costs cannot be recovered. So, there is a break-even point where the ranking changes depending on the call volume, and we need to calculate whether our service is above or below that.
Even after training, there are maintenance costs of evaluation, retraining, and data storage. In cost comparisons, this maintenance cost must be included to obtain the total cost.

Going back to the first two claims, they are both conditionally correct. Tuning becomes cheaper when call volume is high and prompts are greatly reduced, and more expensive when call volume is low or maintenance costs are high. Which one is determined by calculating the number of our services.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: We see value not only in cost, but also in quality improvement. Near the junction, quality differences can dominate the decision.

checks.intro: Think about the monthly cost comparison formula. All you have to do is select the conditions that make the tuning model advantageous.
checks.q: Under what circumstances is a tuned model most likely to have a monthly cost advantage over the base model?
options: When call volume is low and prompt length remains the same
When call volume is small and training cost is high
When the learning cost is excluded from the calculation and only the unit price is compared
When call volume is high and tuning significantly reduces prompts and examples.
checks.explain: Learning is a fixed cost and recall is a variable cost. Tuning shortens the prompt and reduces the token cost per call, resulting in greater gains for larger call volumes.

wrong.0: If the prompts are not reduced, there is no benefit per call and only the learning cost is burdened.
wrong.1: If the call volume is low, it is difficult to recover the fixed learning cost.
wrong.2: If you compare without the training cost, the illusion is that tuning has an advantage.

checks.correctFeedback: That's right. Fixed costs must be recovered when call volume is high and cost per call is reduced.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Consider again the relationship between fixed and variable costs. What needs to be big to recover the fixed costs?

checks.intro: Think about what cost items mean. Just pair items with descriptions.
checks.q: Match tuning cost items with descriptions
right: Costs of running assessments, retraining, and data management
Call volume where two total cost lines intersect
Cost per inference request continues even after tuning
Cost calculated by multiplying the number of dataset tokens by the number of epochs
checks.explain: Learning is a fixed cost, recall is a variable cost, and even after learning, there are maintenance costs of evaluation, re-learning, and storage.
checks.correctFeedback: You have correctly linked the four cost items.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Some things have changed. First, determine whether it is a one-time cost or an ongoing cost.

glossary.def: This is a one-time cost of the tuning operation, proportional to the number of data tokens and the epoch.
This is the cost of operating the tuning model to respond to requests.
This is the fee attached to the input and output tokens for each request.
Operational costs such as evaluation, retraining, and data management.
This is the call volume at which the total cost of the two choices becomes equal.

misconceptions.fact: It depends on how much you can reduce the prompts and the unit cost of your tuning model. Both need to be calculated.

misconceptions.myth: Once learning is over, the cost ends.
misconceptions.fact: There are ongoing inference fees, evaluation, retraining, and data management.
Total costs can be lower if call volume is high and prompts can be significantly reduced or replaced with a smaller model.

closing.lead: The key points of this class are summarized as follows.
points: The total cost is calculated by dividing it into training, serving, recall, and maintenance.
There is a break-even point where the ranking changes depending on the call volume.
Shortening prompts can lower call costs.
Tuning costs don't end with learning.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for you to think about for yourself. It will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Are our call volumes above or below breakeven? What are the numbers needed to make that decision?
